top.title: Christmas on KK is set for Friday, Dec. 11, with 14 businesses on board so far
top.dek: Crafts, cocoa, raffles, Santa and food drives along KK, 5 to 9 p.m., benefiting the Bay View Community Center.
top.body:
Christmas on KK is back. The Bay View Community Center has posted the 2026 edition of the holiday stroll for Friday, Dec. 11, from 5 to 9 p.m., with participating shops and restaurants along Kinnickinnic Avenue hosting treats, kids' crafts, raffles and holiday shopping. Last week neighbors were still asking whether it would return; now there's a date and a lineup.

The center's event listing and flyer name 14 businesses so far: Chippy's, Cozy Collective, Ela Mari Boutique, Fiber Fever, Lion's Tooth, LuLu, Mac's Pet Barkery, the Magnet Factory, Nonfiction Wine, Rush-Mor Records, Sorella, Strange Scene, Tippecanoe Herbs and URSA. Plans include a craft at Chippy's in exchange for a canned-food donation, a hot cocoa bar at Ela Mari, kids' crafts at Strange Scene and a visit with Santa at Tippecanoe Herbs.

Several stops are raising help for the community center: Nonfiction Wine will sell cookie boxes made by local chefs, Sorella plans a featured dish, and URSA and Mac's are tying raffles to food donations for the center's pantry. Organizers say more activities are coming, and businesses that want to join can reach the center's board through the event page. Alderwoman Marina Dimitrijevic shared the event too.
top.source_name: Bay View Community Center on Facebook

openings.title: Buttah and Biscuit shows off the space that will be its first storefront
openings.dek: The biscuit bakery, now cooking out of the Bay View Community Center kitchen, is renovating a shop of its own.
openings.body:
Buttah and Biscuit, the biscuit bakery that has been selling out of the Bay View Community Center's shared kitchen, gave followers a first look inside its own brick-and-mortar space on Saturday. In a video tour, the business said the next few weeks will go to turning the empty room into its first Buttah and Biscuit storefront.

It hasn't said where the shop is or when it will open, so we'll pass that along once it does. In the meantime, its Instagram is the place to watch for updates.

image.alt: An empty storefront with exposed brick and blue walls that will become Buttah and Biscuit's first shop

pets.title: A dog rescue's giving tree is up at Mac's PetDepot on KK
pets.dek: Pick an ornament, buy the item on the back, and the store passes it to JRs Pups-n-stuff.
pets.body:
The rescue group JRs Pups-n-stuff has put up a holiday giving tree at Mac's PetDepot Barkery on Kinnickinnic Avenue. Shoppers grab a paper ornament, buy the supply listed on the back, and leave it at checkout; the store handles the rest, according to a volunteer's post in the Bay View Town Hall group.

The rescue has a second tree at Bad Moon Saloon on Clement Avenue, just south of Bay View, where donors can drop off wishlist items or donate through QR codes on the bin.

spotlight.title: Spotlight: Paloma Taco and Tequila
spotlight.dek: Crunchy pink taco shells, 75-plus tequilas and a whole lot of color under the KinetiK apartments on KK
spotlight.body:
Paloma Taco and Tequila is the most colorful room on lower Kinnickinnic Avenue: a taqueria and tequila bar on the ground floor of the KinetiK apartment building at 2154 S. KK. Think kaleidoscope wallpaper, sunshine-yellow chairs and pendant lights hanging from a turquoise ceiling.

It's run by restaurateur Pattie Ford, who has spent her whole career in restaurants and built a following for her cocktails and infusions at Juniper 61 on North Avenue. Her first Paloma opened in July 2020 a few blocks from there, at 5419 W. North Ave. in Washington Heights. The Bay View location, her second, opened in April 2024 after an eight-month build-out with the design firm Three Sixty. At about 2,300 square feet, it's more than twice the size of the original, according to the Milwaukee Business Journal, as reported by TMJ4.

Tacos are the main event, roughly 10 kinds from carne asada to crispy tofu and tuna poke, on flour or corn tortillas, Paloma's signature crunchy pink shell, or "naked" over lettuce. There are also elote cups, loaded fries, quesadillas, the Big Paloma Torta and the Taco Pocket, a playful riff on a fast-food classic. Vegan, vegetarian and gluten-free dishes are marked on the menu, and brunch items run until 2 p.m. The bar pours more than 75 tequilas, and there's even a dog menu: a warm tortilla with banana and peanut butter.

Paloma also caters, sells gift certificates and runs a rewards program. Its Bay View spot is one of a cluster of newer restaurants and bars at KinetiK, alongside neighbors like 17th Ward.

What's new: happy hour now runs all day on Sundays and Mondays, plus weekdays from 4 to 6 p.m. Paloma says it's taking $1 off its THC drinks until they're gone, to clear its stock before a ban takes effect. A new veggie sandwich (or the same build with New York strip) is a Bay View exclusive, and a paint-and-sip night is on the calendar for Monday, Dec. 14, at 6:30 p.m.

Paloma Taco and Tequila, 2154 S. Kinnickinnic Ave. (the website lists 2156), 414-212-8978. Open Monday through Wednesday 11 a.m. to 9 p.m., Thursday 4 to 9 p.m., Friday and Saturday 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., Sunday 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. palomatacoandtequila.com, @palomabayview on Instagram.

buzz.headline: A possum rescue wants your freezer-burned meat
buzz.body: Cleaning out the freezer before the Thanksgiving groceries arrive? A neighbor who collects food for a possum rescue says she'll be parked outside the Starbucks at KK and Oklahoma on Sunday, Nov. 29, from noon to 4, with a cooler on the sidewalk for expired or freezer-burned meat, seafood, cheese, veggies and fruit (no spices, please). Got a full grocery bag or more? She'll arrange a pickup. The burning question in the comments: will an actual possum be there?

history.title: Armistice week, 1918: 10,000 Bay View marchers fill Humboldt Park
history.text: In November 1918, days after the armistice, more than 10,000 Bay View residents marched down KK and Logan to Humboldt Park to honor the neighborhood's soldiers.
history.body:
World War I had been over for less than a week when Bay View put on what the Milwaukee Sentinel called the most elaborate of the city's observances. On Sunday, Nov. 17, 1918, after a week of noisy celebrating across Milwaukee, neighborhoods turned to a more serious ritual: unveiling service flags, the banners with a star for each local man in uniform, and dedicating honor rolls of names.

Bay View's turnout was the biggest. The Sentinel reported that more than 10,000 residents paraded along Kinnickinnic and Logan avenues to Humboldt Park, with Boy Scouts carrying Allied flags at the head of the line. A Scout drum corps, the band of the Solvay Coke company, about 250 members of the State Guard and Spanish-American War veterans with their own drum corps marched too, followed by more Scout troops and crowds of children.

The crowd was so large that organizers changed their plans. The neighborhood's service flag was unveiled temporarily in Humboldt Park, with a promise that it would later fly at the corner of Logan and Kinnickinnic avenues. Speakers struck one theme over and over, the paper said: the country could never do enough to honor the men who had served and those who had died.

The park would stay at the center of Bay View's memory of the war. A few months later, a neighborhood committee even asked the city to rename it after Gen. John J. Pershing (look for that story later this week). The name never changed, but more than a century later Humboldt Park is still where Bay View gathers, from Chill on the Hill concerts to holiday events.
